objectives: Segment taught b CVC words into phonemes.
Map each phoneme to the correct grapheme.
Spell b CVC words from spoken dictation.
Self-correct initial and short-vowel spelling errors.
concepts: CVC spelling requires ordered phoneme segmentation.
Short vowels determine the middle grapheme.
Reading back the spelling supports self-correction.

definitions.definition: Separate a spoken word into its individual phonemes.
A letter or letter group representing a speech sound.
Using phoneme knowledge to write the graphemes in a spoken word.

commonMistakes: Replacing b with d or p.
Writing letter names instead of graphemes.

basic: Spell taught b CVC words from dictation.
conceptual: Identify the phoneme represented by each grapheme.
application: Repair CVC spelling errors by isolating the incorrect sound.
higherOrderThinking: Explain how changing the middle vowel changes a CVC spelling.
mixedReview: Mix b CVC spelling with previously taught consonants and short vowels.

formulaOrFactBank: CVC spelling = phoneme sequence mapped to graphemes in order.
mistakeBasedRevision: If spelling is wrong, say the word slowly and identify the mismatched sound.
weakTopicRevision: Practise the weakest short-vowel pattern with fresh b CVC words.

activities.name: Sound boxes
steps: Push one counter for each phoneme.
Write one grapheme for each sound.

activities.name: Vowel contrast dictation
steps: Say two similar b CVC words.

activities.name: Spell and repair
steps: Compare each grapheme with the sound sequence.

outcomes: Learner segments taught b CVC words accurately.
Learner maps phonemes to graphemes in order.
Learner spells taught b CVC words and self-corrects common errors.

questions.question: What letter represents /b/ at the start of “bed”?
What letter represents the middle sound in “big”?
What is the final letter in “rub”?
A learner hears /b/ /æ/ /g/. Which word should they spell?
What should a learner do before writing a dictated CVC word?
options: Say and segment each phoneme in order.

questions.question: A learner writes “bed” for “bad.” Which sound needs checking?
A learner writes “dig” for “big.” Which sound should be corrected?
Why should the learner read the completed spelling back?
options: It helps check whether the written graphemes match the spoken sounds.
It removes the need to segment.

questions.question: A learner spells “bug” correctly but confuses “bag” and “beg.” What is the best next practice?
options: Contrast the short-vowel sounds and spell fresh dictated words.

questions.question: After accurate spelling of taught b CVC words, what should follow?
options: Controlled b word-family reading and sentence spelling
